title: Patel Brothers, Apna Bazar, and the Big-Box Revolution in Indian Grocery
excerpt: Indian-American supermarkets are leaving their strip-mall roots behind, moving into former ShopRites and Buy Buy Babys with pharmacies, cafes, and 70,000 square feet of ambition.
body:
Walk into the new Patidar Supermarket in Bridgewater, New Jersey, and you might forget you are in an Indian grocery store at all. Housed in a former Buy Buy Baby, the big-box location is more than three times the size of Patidar's original North Brunswick storefront, complete with a pharmacy, a cafe, organic produce, and an expanded array of mainstream American groceries alongside imported Indian staples.

It is not an anomaly. It is the new normal.

## The Great Indian Grocery Upgrade

Across the northeastern United States, Indian-American supermarkets are undergoing a transformation that mirrors the community's own evolution. Patel Brothers, the largest Indian supermarket chain in the country, has opened one of its biggest stores in Hamilton, New Jersey, and is working on another in a former ShopRite in Piscataway. These are not the cramped, fluorescent-lit aisles of the old neighborhood Indian store. They are spacious, well-designed, and increasingly designed to attract shoppers who are not Indian at all.

Apna Bazar, a fast-growing chain with 22 locations across the Northeast, has announced plans to expand on Long Island and open its largest store yet — a 70,000-square-foot former Stop & Shop in Shrewsbury, Massachusetts. That is the size of a mid-range Whole Foods.

## Why Now

The numbers tell the story. The Indian-American population has grown to nearly 5 million, making it one of the fastest-growing demographic groups in the United States. But the bigger shift is cultural. Second-generation Indian Americans are grocery shopping differently from their parents — they want the atta flour and the avocados, the Haldiram's namkeen and the organic kale, all under one roof.

These new stores are designed for that dual identity. A Patel Brothers in 2026 looks less like the ethnic grocery stores of the 1990s and more like a Wegmans with a better spice aisle. Cafe seating areas, upscale decor, fresh sushi counters alongside chaat stations — the format is a deliberate bid to be the primary grocery destination, not a supplementary stop.

## The Competitive Landscape

The expansion is happening against a backdrop of broader grocery industry disruption. Online grocery sales are projected to grow at an 11.6% compound annual rate through 2028, and mainstream chains are investing heavily in delivery and curbside pickup. Indian grocers are responding: many of the new locations offer online ordering and delivery, competing not just with each other but with Amazon Fresh, Instacart, and the growing Indian grocery delivery startups.

The grocery chains are also benefiting from a cultural tailwind. Indian food is America's fastest-growing cuisine category, according to Yelp search data, with surging interest in tiffin services, regional specialties, and pantry staples like ghee and paneer. Mainstream retailers like Walmart and Costco have expanded their Indian food sections, but dedicated Indian grocers still hold the advantage in depth and authenticity.

## What This Means for NRIs

For first-generation Indian Americans who remember the days of driving an hour to the nearest Indian store, the transformation is remarkable. But it also reflects a community that is no longer content to be a niche market. A 70,000-square-foot Apna Bazar in Massachusetts is a statement of permanence — a signal that Indian-American retail is here to stay, and it is done being small.

## What's Next

The big-box Indian grocery model is still largely a Northeast phenomenon, concentrated in New Jersey, New York, and Massachusetts where Indian-American populations are densest. But with chains like Patel Brothers already operating in 20 states, the format is likely to spread to Texas, California, and the Midwest. For NRIs in those markets, the days of the tiny strip-mall Indian store may be numbered — and what replaces them will look a lot more like home.
author: Diaspora Desk
